## How an upgrade decides, file by file

There used to be a table here saying which paths were yours outright, which were
replaced wholesale, and which were both. The table was a hand-written answer to a
question the machinery can measure, and a layout change upstream would have needed
it rewritten. It is gone, and what replaces it is the ordinary git three-way merge:

- **A file you never touched takes the new version, silently.** Whatever upstream
  did — added, changed, deleted — happens to your tree as if you had done it.
- **A file you edited, upstream did not touch, keeps your words.** The upgrade
  does not restore a default over your work.
- **A file you both changed is the one thing that stops.** The update applies the
  release on a branch, runs the merge, and where your edit and upstream's change
  land on the same lines the file comes out carrying conflict markers that name
  both sides. The pull request stands, nothing merges, and resolving it is
  [yours to make](tasks/move-to-a-newer-release.md) — by hand, or by asking an
  agent on that pull request.

No path is special-cased. Whether something collides is measured from what your
tree actually holds, at update time — so a file you customised in a directory the
template mostly owns behaves exactly like one in a directory you own outright, and
a directory upstream adds needs no new rule to be handled correctly.

**Paths are not settings.** No key says where any of this lives, and that is a
decision rather than an omission: `.github/atomaton/README.md` gives the three
====
## `agents.on_update_conflict`

```yaml
update:
  on_new_release: pr-agent
agents:
  on_update_conflict: engineer
```

The agent started on an update pull request that stopped on a conflict — the third
of the [ways to take a newer release](../runtime/tasks/move-to-a-newer-release.md),
and the one place where a run nobody asked for is started on work that has to be
judged.

It is required only when `update.on_new_release` is `pr-agent`, and it is the only
key in this section that is not required outright: until the mode asks for an agent,
nothing reads a name. Set it and leave the mode alone and it is still checked against
the definitions that exist, because a name that resolves to nothing is the same
failure whenever the mode is turned on. The pair is checked as a pair — a `pr-agent`
mode with no name fails the pull request's own check, and the sentence names both
keys, because either one is the edit that fixes it.

It is a different question from `on_config_finding`, and the difference is the shape
of the condition: that one is `atoma` reporting a defect in a tools file, which

/**
 * Start the agent `update.on_new_release: pr-agent` names, on the update pull

 *
 * The mode is a policy for the collision, so this is called by the update run itself
 * -- whoever started it. A person's `!upgrade` that collides starts the agent on a
 * repository that chose `pr-agent`, because the repository chose what happens on a
 * collision, not what happens on a comment.
 *
 * `plan.kept` never reaches here: the plan declined to decide, and a person decides.
 * Only actual conflict markers do, which is the same line the update already draws
 * between the two kinds of stop.
 *
 * The directive comment is this dispatch's marker AND its run's ask, the way the
 * post-merge re-invocation does it -- tagged `include`, because it is the first
 * message the resolving agent reads and it is what tells it what to do.
 *
 * One limit is the agent's rather than the merge's: GitHub refuses a workflow file
 * written with a token that holds no `workflow` scope (#650), and the agent's holds
 * none. The directive says so and the agent is started anyway -- the conflict is the
 * whole input a resolver needs, and a pull request whose conflicts mix the two kinds
 * is half-resolvable rather than not started at all. Withholding the workflow paths
 * here would mean deciding, before the files are read, which collision needs a
 * person.
 */
export function dispatchUpdateConflictAgent(repo: string, prNumber: number, agent: string): boolean {
  return (
    dispatchDirective(repo, prNumber, agent, {
      context: `the update pull request #${prNumber} stopped on a conflict, so ${agent} was to resolve it`,
      type: "pr",
      directive:
        "Atomaton: this pull request takes a newer release onto this tree and stopped where the two " +
        "sides disagree — the files listed above carry conflict markers naming both. Resolve them, " +
        "keeping what this repository wrote where it was deliberate and taking what the release " +
        "changed everywhere else, and say in your report which side you took for each file and why. " +
        "One limit on where you can write: a conflicted path under `.github/workflows/` is a " +
        "person's, because GitHub refuses a workflow file written with your token and the push " +
        "carrying it would be rejected. Leave those files' markers exactly as they are, resolve " +
        "the others, and name the workflow paths in your report so a person can finish them. A " +
        "conflict that mixes the two kinds is the same: the workflow files stay for the person, " +
        "and you resolve the rest. " +
        "Nothing merges from here: the repository's checks run on the resolved tree, and the merge is " +
        "a person's.",
    }) === "dispatched"
  );
}

Committing markers is the documented design — both sides visible on the pull request — and it works for every file except the one the machinery reads to know what to do. `.github/atomaton/config.yaml` declares the checks, `environment.setup_commands`, the merge policy, the agent names and each tool server's reach. - `plan_checks.ts --arm pull-request` failed → the pull request's checks were never planned (measured on the bot commit `807126cf`: `plan-pull-request-checks`, `atomaton-tools` and `atomaton-check` all red, while `plan-default-branch-checks` passed, because that arm reads the default branch).
- `run_environment_setup.ts` failed before any agent could start, so the documented way out — "ask an agent on that pull request to resolve them" — was not reachable for this file at all.
- A re-run reads the same commit, so it fails the same way.

So the fix is not "stop writing markers": it is **this path is never written with them**. The tree keeps its own copy; the two sides `git merge-file` produced are carried into the pull request's body; the update still stops at that pull request, because choosing between two versions of a setting is a person's call (kept separate from this change, as asked).
